## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/03.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Academic Recovery in 2024
• The availability of 2024 SBA data allows Hawaii to update
 COVID-19 recovery analyses.
• Spring 2024 marks the third year since the pandemic began
 and this is the third report:
 • Summer 2021: Academic Impact
 • Summer 2022: Academic Recovery Year 1
 • Summer 2023: Academic Recovery Year 2
 • Summer 2024: Academic Recovery Year 3

 3</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/04.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Two Types of Recovery in 2024: System &amp; Student
• We elaborate on the results from the previous recovery analyses in two
 ways:
 • System level recovery: Is the education system supporting rates of
 learning that are comparable to what it was prior to the pandemic?
 • Student level recovery: Are students achieving at levels that are
 comparable to what they were prior to the pandemic?
• Previously, we focused mostly on system-level recovery: examining rates
 of learning in 2021 and 2022 compared to those prior to the pandemic.
• We continue examining system level analyses but also focus on student-
 level recovery.

 4</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/05.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Two Types of Recovery: System &amp; Student
• System-level recovery
 • Comparison of 2019 and 2024 same-grade student growth: We
 examine the change in baseline student growth (SGPs) for 2019
 students and 2024 students utilizing coefficient matrices derived
 from pre-pandemic cohorts of students.
• Student-level recovery
 • Comparison of 2019 to 2024 same-grade achievement: We
 examine the equi-percentile change in achievement for 2019
 students and 2024 students at same-grade

 5</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/06.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Student-level recovery
• It is critical to understand that recovery of the system does not imply student level
 recovery
• Because students’ rates of learning slowed so dramatically during the pandemic, rates of
 learning necessary to catch students up to where they would have been would have to be
 equally dramatic (in the positive direction)
• As of 2024, 4 cohorts of students have exited the system (via graduation) achieving at
 levels, on average, below where they would have been had the pandemic not occurred.
• The following figures illustrate the extent to which student attainment is behind 2019
 attainment levels.
• Comparison to 2019 attainment levels is a “low bar” for comparison:
 • Attainment levels in 2024, had the pandemic not occurred, would almost certainly
 have been higher than 2019 levels (based on “typical” rates of yearly improvement)

 6</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/09.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Why Baseline SGPs?
• There was a question of why one needs to look at baseline referenced SGPs
 instead of, for example, scale score gains. There are several reasons.
 • SGPs are the growth metric that the state of Hawaii has been using for more
 than a decade.
 • SGPs are readily interpretable probabilistically whereas gain scores are not.
 • Quantile regression (on which SGPs are based) is invariant to mono-tone
 transformations of scale (equivariant to mono-tone transformations of scale).
 OLS regression, for example, is not. See Koenker (2005, p. 38)
 • Gain scores (which can be calculated since SBA is vertically scaled) are
 dependent upon: Content area, grade, prior level of achievement.
 • Gain scores were largely discredited as an effective means of communicating
 change. For example, no state uses them as a growth model.

 9</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/10.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Status based impact versus growth?
• There was another question about the equivalence of status change and
 growth change.
 • Previously, I justified this change heuristically by noting that growth
 change (deceleration from 2021) had to lead to status change.
 • That is, decreases in learning (as quantified by growth) necessarily lead
 to decreases in achievement.
 • Also, this is empirically verified based upon two years of data plotted for
 several states across grade and content areas show a correlation of 0.91.
 • This relationship isn’t a function of content area or year but a
 relationship between status change and conditional status (i.e., growth)
 change.
 10</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/15.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Phase Year 1
• Student growth (baseline referenced to pre-pandemic rates of learning) was
 examined by content area and grade as well as for the major student
 demographic subgroups.
• Achievement (Student Recovery) and Growth (System Recovery) were
 characterized in three ways:
 • Lagging: Behind pre-pandemic levels (attainment or growth)
 • On Par: About the same as pre-pandemic levels (attainment or growth)
 • Leading: Ahead of pre-pandemic levels (attainment or growth)
• Because learning slowed during the initial phase of the pandemic (2020 to
 2021), to make up for those losses, learning must accelerate to rates above
 normal (i.e., leading)
 15</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/18.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Year 1
• Analysis of 2022 SBA data indicated several positive trends in Hawai’i to be happy
 about.
• In both ELA and mathematics, learning acceleration was at least as much to be
 considered stabilization and in many cases could be considered as genuine
 recovery.
• Compared to a dozen other states that the Center conducts these analyses,
 Hawai’i comes out as the best in terms of pandemic recovery.
• Despite a robust recovery, students remain slightly behind 2019 levels in ELA and
 further behind in mathematics.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/19.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Year 1: Qualitative Investigation
• HIDOE commissioned a study, based upon an initial ROI investigation based upon money spent during the pandemic
 to help students.
• We identified 15 schools to investigate (via 90 minute zoom interviews) more thoroughly based upon three patterns:
 • High impact/high recovery
 • High impact/little to no recovery
 • Low impact/high recovery
• My colleague Jeri Thompson and I investigated this recovery, focusing on schools demonstrating large rates of
 recovery that continued through 2023.
• As was reported previously, Hawaii, overall experienced a robust recovery in 2022 in rates of student learning —
 much more so than other states.
• Our interviews failed to identify a program or intervention responsible for what we observed at the 15 schools we
 investigated.
• More on year 2.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/24.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Year 2
• Analysis of 2023 SBA data indicates two things:
 • Rates of learning, on average, are slightly exceeding or at pre-pandemic rates of
 growth. That is, the system has recovered, and then some.
 • Student attainment, on average, is still lagging behind because rates of learning have
 not accelerated enough to catch students up. That is, students have not recovered.
• In both ELA and mathematics, learning acceleration from the lows of the pandemic would
 be considered, on average, to be system stabilization.
• System stabilization (a return to normal rates of learning) will be insufficient to catch
 students up.
• Averages can obscure important heterogeneity:

 24</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/25.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Year 2: Qualitative Investigation
• Upon reflection of our initial findings, we hypothesize that the robust recovery was driven by cultural factors more so than programmatic
 factors.
• To investigate further, we identified 5 schools that continued to experience superior rates of growth to those demonstrated prior to the onset
 of the pandemic. 4 of those schools agreed to a full day meeting to discuss impact and recovery due to the pandemic.
 • Kalihi-waena Elementary
 • Mililani ‘Ike Elementary
 • Waipahu Elementary
 • Mililani Middle
• Our hypothesis is that these schools thrived due to efforts to maintain strong relationships during the COVID-19 crisis. Specifically, we believe
 Hawaii’s culture of ‘Ohana led to:
 • strong relational networks among students, teachers, parents, and the broader community that supported emotional and academic
 resilience.enhanced collaboration between schools and families, fostering a sense of mutual responsibility for student success.
 • a focus on belonging and cultural identity, which helped students navigate challenges and stay connected to their educational journey.
 • a shared community ethos where collective well-being was prioritized, enabling targeted and empathetic support for struggling students
 and families.
 • enduring trust and communication frameworks that were established during the pandemic and maintained in the recovery period.</div>
```

## {.archive-slide background-image="slides/47.webp" background-size="contain" background-color="#14140f"}

```{=html}
<div class="archive-text">Recovery Year 3
• Analysis of 2023 SBA data indicates two things:
 • Rates of learning, on average, are returning to pre-pandemic levels. Elevated rates of
 learning observed in 2022 and 2023 are moderating.
 • Student attainment, on average, is still slightly behind pre-pandemic levels.
• In both ELA and mathematics, learning acceleration from the lows of the pandemic would
 be considered, on average, to be system stabilization.
• System stabilization (a return to normal rates of learning) will be insufficient to catch
 students up.
• Averages can obscure important heterogeneity: For example, between males and females
 in mathematics

 47</div>
```
